newsitem.title: ALBANIA: FEATURE - Albanians hope vote will ease economic anomalies.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Albanians hope vote will ease economic anomalies.

text.p: Alush Celhaga hopes the left-wing victory in Albania's election last month will bring him at least peace and quiet if not a small measure of prosperity.

As the incoming government grapples with the aftermath of months of chaos, there seems little hope that he will get early relief from the poverty and social anomalies that abound in the bustling town of Kavaje -- and throughout the country.

Seven years after haphazard capitalism replaced one of Europe's harshest communist governments, Celhaga performs a vital service on market days for farmers who rely on donkeys to bring oversize loads of produce to town.

He pockets the equivalent of 15 U.S. cents for every animal entrusted to him in an enclosure. With 30-odd donkeys filling it to capacity and a "spillover" lot taking in more on an adjacent street, he stands little chance of getting rich quick when the cash is totted up alongside his monthly pension of $20.

"With only three million people, our country could have been on top of everybody. We could have been a second Switzerland," he said. "All we can do now is hope that things get at least a little bit better."
Like countless thousands, Celhaga lost what little he had scraped together -- the equivalent of $600 -- in one of five pyramid investment schemes that folded earlier this year.
Voters last month overwhelmingly rejected President Sali Berisha's right-wing Democratic Party and the "capitalism without banks" which many commentators said he produced during five years in power.
They had few qualms about voting for the Socialists, reformed heirs to dictator Enver Hoxha's communists, giving them a huge parliamentary majority.
Even Kavaje, with a fierce anti-communist tradition 50 km (30 miles) southwest of the capital Tirana, deserted the Democrats. Party leader Tritan Shehu was one of three to lose their seats.
Pro-market policies made Berisha popular after he came to power in 1992 and he was lionised by the United States when Albania posted some of Eastern Europe's best economic results.

The proliferation of the investment schemes with tantalising, high returns further burnished his image until the collapses. More than 1,500 people died in the ensuing violence and Berisha was forced to call the election.
ANOMALIES
There are plenty of other anomalies in Kavaje.
Reshat, a butcher, shook his head as he removed French chickens, carefully packed in plastic, from his display case.
The chickens have flooded Kavaje shops, each pack selling for the equivalent of $2.50, since a local battery poultry farm went broke and shut down.

"Can you imagine anything quite so absurd -- a country with a farming tradition like ours importing chicken? I've even seen Bulgarian peppers in the market," said Reshat, a copy of the Koran perched prominently on a shelf above his till.

Reshat set about improving the state-run butcher's shop when communism collapsed. That meant importing a refrigerator, display case and a meat grinder from Italy -- an hour's flight over the Adriatic Sea -- as they were unavailable in Albania.
"What's missing now is discipline and basic respect for human life," he said.

"For 50 years under communism no one thought about profit or the sweat required to produce things. When the system changed things started out well, but the mentality was wrong. What good is money if you don't have peace?"
Frenetic activity on Kavaje's main business street, lined with farmers selling fruit, sunflower seeds or olives, peters out on rutted roads leading to a vast, ghost-like glassworks.

A watchman on duty must be awakened to gain admittance to a courtyard littered with rusting trucks and a loader, their tyres all flat. Further on, the plant's smokestack is cracked, weeds choke outbuildings and, the most bitter of ironies, dozens of smashed window panes remain unrepaired.
Cheaper imported glass has reduced staff to 12 from a payroll of 2,000 only 18 months ago. The last workers face redundancy once buyers are found for remaining stock.
TOWN SPARED LOOTING
Local officials said Kavaje's tradition as a town of hard-working businessmen spared it the disorder and looting that destroyed Albanians' already limited faith in post-communist institutions.
But shopkeepers said they were afraid to leave their premises unattended and even a short stay in the town showed their concern was well-grounded.
Regulars at one of the bars dotting the main street hardly batted an eyelid as a motorbike pulled up and a man on the back fired a Kalashnikov rifle into the air, his face breaking into a broad grin.
A second man opened fire from the billiard hall across the street. No one seemed to know why and, as it was over quickly, it mattered little.
With calm restored, the bar talk was of more anomalies.
Agron Shima, in his fifties, said he had at least managed to find steady work with a German firm.
"Every day I take home enough wages to buy four of these," he said, pushing together bottles of mineral water from adjacent tables.

Next to him, Ismail Kamberi said people were unwilling to undertake any risk with ill-defined post-communist rules -- particularly claims to pre-1944 ownership of land in a country where 60 percent of the people live in the countryside.
"We had 50 years with Hoxha and the communists denying the people their land. Now we have total confusion over who owns shops, apartment buildings, everything," he said.
"This is the the biggest danger to rebuilding society. Both the Democratic Party and the Socialists have refused to tackle it for fear of antagonising people."
A third patron, Xhemal Bello, said his family owned 600 olive trees and a string of meadows in the southern port of Sarande with no immediate prospect of claiming them back.
For donkey attendant Celhaga, such discussions remain academic.
"I am thankful that I have a job that brings in some money," he said. "Some people talk about going off to Italy or Greece. I'm going to stay here."
